name: blender-kiln
description: Text or photo to game-ready GLB through Blender MCP
readme:
blender-kiln — The 3D Asset Forge

**Describe an object, or show a photo of it, and get back a clean 3D model you can edit, ship in a game or on the web, animate, or print.** kiln is a Claude Code skill on top of a Blender MCP server. The MCP server gives Claude hands in Blender; kiln gives it the production method — sourcing, modelling, cleanup, texturing from CC0 scans, optimization, validation, export — and measures the file it ships. It runs on both servers: [ahujasid's `mcp-for-blender`](https://github.com/ahujasid/mcp-for-blender) and the Blender Foundation's [official Blender Lab MCP](https://projects.blender.org/lab/blender_mcp), the server behind Claude's Blender connector. Cited in 3DCodeBench: Benchmarking Agentic Procedural 3D Modeling Via Code (Google DeepMind, USC, 2026), §1.

From one photo each, no marketplace, no AI generation: scripted in Blender, textured from CC0 scans, measured against the real object. Shape scores against the real assets: 0.888, 0.948, 0.729 — all three with review rounds; how they are measured.

## Quickstart ``` /plugin marketplace add elithril/blender-kiln /plugin install blender-kiln@blender-kiln /kiln setup /kiln A hanging iron lantern for a medieval inn, stylized, for the web ``` `/kiln setup` detects Blender, the MCP server and the optional tools, and says what is missing — see [Requirements](#requirements). Then, for example: ``` /kiln Rebuild the lamp in ./lamp.png as a game asset /kiln optimize ./generated.glb # a GLB from anywhere: lighter, checked /kiln animate SK_Cat.glb walk, idle /kiln A 90 mm windmill for my FDM printer /kiln studio # look at the models, pin notes, let Claude act on them ``` ## What kiln does Every model comes out clean, named, at real size, on the ground, compressed for the web (Draco, WebP) and checked — as GLB, FBX, USDZ or STL. On top of that, 3.0 adds: ### Kiln Studio — look at your models, pin a note, let Claude fix it

A real session from the 3.0 bench: the note was pinned in the page, Claude made the change and replied on it.
How it works: watch a real session ▶

A local page that shows every model in your project. Pin a note on a spot — *"the ring is too small to hang it"* — press **Work on it with Claude**, and the change lands in the model, with Claude's reply and a before/after on the note. Studio also exports for games and AR in seconds, and shows the model in AR on your iPhone through a QR code. From the terminal, Claude sees the model you have open in Studio and can turn it, compare it and present it on a second screen. Measured: a note addressed in one pass, nothing else moved, for $0.69 of API-equivalent usage.
Everything Studio does A local page for looking at what kiln made, telling it what to change, and asking Claude from the page itself. `/kiln studio` starts it on your project folder (or reuses the one running): every `.glb .gltf .fbx .obj .usdz .3mf .stl` under it shows up, and kiln's `_original` … `_final` stages are one model you can switch between. - **Look** — Lit, Unlit, Clay, Normals, UV checker, Faces (back faces red), wireframe, sizes in metres, bones, animation clips with a scrubber; the previous version beside the current one. - **Annotate** — pin a note on a spot (it records the point in Blender coordinates, the object and material hit, the camera, a screenshot and a close-up) or write one about the whole model. - **Ask Claude from the page** — with "Ask Claude from Studio" on, the page runs Claude Code itself (`claude -p`, on its own Blender, never yours): "Work on them with Claude" addresses every open note, a conversation per model and one for the project, *New model* asks for a model from a sentence or a photo. Safe calls pass; anything else waits for your OK in the page, and paid generation asks unless you set it to Auto in Settings. Measured on the bench: a note asking for a ring twice as big, addressed in one pass — ×1.9, nothing else moved, the note answered — for $0.69 of API-equivalent usage (official Lab MCP: $0.73). Or run `/kiln studio` in your terminal: Claude reads the open notes, changes the model, re-exports and replies on each. - **Claude in your terminal sees what Studio shows** — installed as a plugin, kiln brings a small MCP server, `kiln-studio`, with nothing more to set up (a standalone-skill clone does not register it). Say *"fix this"* or *"what am I looking at"* and Claude reads the model open in the page, its stage, the camera and the note picked, and can grab the image you see. It drives the page too: open a model, turn the view to a note's, switch to clay or normals, a before/after against the previous version, play a clip, and a present mode for a second screen. It replies on notes and leaves its own, and makes variations and finishes when you ask; it never touches a model file itself. Tools and when they are called: [`references/studio.md` § 11](plugin/references/studio.md#11-the-kiln-studio-mcp-server--what-the-user-is-looking-at-and-driving-studio). - **Outputs** — Web, Game, AR and 3D print for each model. Game (FBX) and AR (a GLB and a USDZ that passes `usdchecker --arkit`) are made by Studio itself, in seconds, without Claude. *Download* zips the outputs you pick with a sheet: each file's size and use, the licences. - **On your phone** — a QR code shows the model in AR on an iPhone (AR Quick Look), on the same Wi-Fi, through a read-only link that expires after 15 minutes. Android: not tried yet. - **Variations and finishes** — new models from a copy of this one ("the same in rusted iron"), one Claude run each, several at once if you allow it; finishes are kept in one file (`KHR_materials_variants`) and the AR view lets you pick one. - **Check** — the Checks tab reads the file in plain words, each with how to fix it: triangles against the detail tier, size and ground contact, texture sizes, compression, the licences the log records, and the fidelity measure against the reference photo. - **Watch it built** — once the brief is confirmed, the page opens the model kiln is building and reloads it after each phase; a dot per model shows what kiln is on. - Every command by name (⌘K), seven themes (high contrast among them), English and French, a playable tutorial on an example model, a tip the first time you meet each feature. **No extra service.** Studio is a Python standard-library server bound to `127.0.0.1`; only the phone link reaches your local network. Claude runs on the account you choose in Settings — your Claude subscription by default; another Claude account or an API key are supported but **not yet tested with a real one**. Notes live in the project's `.kiln-studio/`, ready to commit with the models. [`references/studio.md`](plugin/references/studio.md) is the reference.
### 3D printing — models that actually print

Printed on a Bambu Lab P1S, PLA, 0.2 mm layers, as kiln exported them: the windmill (2 parts, 90 mm), the forge of the logo (3 parts, 70 mm), the lighthouse (50 mm), the Art Deco box with its bayonet lid (Ø 62 mm).

Say it will be printed — FDM or resin, a height, your printer's colours — and kiln models for the printer from the first primitive: closed solids at size, walls thick enough, a flat base, parts that fit together, one file per colour. Every file is checked, with PrusaSlicer as a second opinion. In the bench, the 3.0 passed both prints the 2.2.0 had half-failed; four objects kiln modelled were printed as exported, on a Bambu Lab P1S.
How print mode works, and its limits Say it will be printed — FDM or resin, a height, your printer's colours — and kiln models **for the printer from the first primitive**: at size, in closed solids joined into one volume, walls thick enough (0.8 mm FDM, 0.5 mm resin), a flat base, overhangs designed out where nobody looks, relief as geometry, and in several parts when one would print in the air — the windmill above is a body and its sails, laid flat, each checked on its own. STL in millimetres. Every STL ends with [`tools/print_check.py`](plugin/tools/print_check.py): open and non-manifold edges, normals, held and floating parts, walls, overhangs, loss against the original, the smallest scale you can shrink it to in the slicer, and PrusaSlicer as a second opinion ([`references/print.md`](plugin/references/print.md)).

Measured on sessions given the skill and nothing else: a dog house and a lighthouse from a brief, a pumpkin and a ghost from photos, the windmill, and this teapot from three museum photos — printable, and like what was asked. **Stylised figures, not likenesses.** Two cats — one held by the ghost, one from a real cat's photo — passed every check and were unacceptable to look at. A stylised figure is another matter: a session made a cartoon dragon from one flat drawing, in four colour parts, from **metaball families and one voxel remesh**, and a fresh session then made a cartoon fox the same way. So print mode builds a stylised figure that way, and says at CONFIG that a realistic likeness of a real animal or person is out of reach of scripted modelling. ### A model you made: flatten it, then check it

A model finished by hand often has faces that should be flat and are not, and sits a degree off. [`tools/flatten.py`](plugin/tools/flatten.py) makes nearly flat faces exactly flat and lays the base on the bed — on the windmill above, **629 mm of first layer become 3,317** — and touches nothing else: curves, folds, bevels and real slopes stay, no vertex moves past the tolerance, the input is never overwritten. ``` /kiln inspect model.stl # print mode: print_check's verdict /kiln cleanup model.stl # print mode: flatten.py, then print_check again, before and after shown ``` ### Limits - **Printed, four of them.** The forge, the lighthouse, the Art Deco box and the windmill were printed as kiln exported them, on a Bambu Lab P1S in PLA ([photos](#3d-printing--models-that-actually-print)). The box's bayonet lid turns, locks and holds with the box upside down. The fit test print was not printed; the rest was checked by PrusaSlicer 2.9.6 and by renders, not on a bed. - **FDM, checked with PrusaSlicer's default profile.** No resin slicing, no orientation search, no support generation, no build-volume check. - **Scaled down in the slicer, a model loses its thin walls.** `print_check` says how far — "do not shrink below 40 %" for the windmill's body, 67 % for the lighthouse. - **Parts are glued or pressed, never moving.** 0.2 mm a side is a usual clearance, not measured here; [`tools/fit_coupon.py`](plugin/tools/fit_coupon.py) writes the test print that measures it on your printer. - **Decorative objects, not mechanical parts.** A bracket, or a box whose lid must close, belongs in a CAD tool (build123d, CadQuery, OpenSCAD). - **No multi-material file.** A colour is painted, or printed as its own part. - **Self-intersections are counted, not repaired**, and `flatten.py` does not fill holes. The full list is in [`references/print.md`](plugin/references/print.md) § What it does not check. The teapot photo is the Auckland War Memorial Museum's, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
### From a photo — rebuilt in Blender, measured against the real object

Every panel is a file the session itself wrote while rebuilding the ammo box above — nothing re-staged.

Give it a photo and kiln rebuilds the object by script, textures it from CC0 scans, and measures its silhouette and materials against the photo before shipping. Against the real 3D object the photo was taken of: an ammo box at **0.948** with review rounds (0.936 on the bench, before them), a hurricane lantern at **0.888** (0.885 before them), **0.946** when kiln finishes a TRELLIS.2 mesh of the photo ([the numbers](#measured-not-claimed)).
The five steps 1. **Read the photo before modeling.** An inventory of every part and how it meets the next, from enlarged crops; the real size, the camera's height and angle — asked, or stated as assumptions. Given a 3D mesh generated from the same photo, its proportions are measured instead ([TRELLIS.2, locally](plugin/references/ai-generation.md)) — never shipped. 2. **Texture from scans, not noise.** A Poly Haven CC0 texture set of the material family, chosen by eye against the photo, tinted to its palette, worn by the form. 3. **Measure against the photo.** [`plugin/tools/fidelity_check.py`](plugin/tools/fidelity_check.py) renders the model at the photo's camera under a studio light and lists the gaps — silhouette per height band, materials, metal that cannot exist. 4. **Look at every joint.** Each end of a long part that touches another is rendered alone: a part that joins another enters it. 5. **Ship, and measure the file that ships.** Optimized (Draco, WebP), validated, re-measured as a GLB — what the user gets, not the `.blend`.
### Animate, and characters that bend

`/kiln animate` picks the route from the subject: ready-made humanoid moves (22 motions), text-to-motion for bipeds and winged creatures, a measured walk and idle for quadrupeds, keyed parts for objects. Characters are built as one skin and rigged by a learned auto-rig: skin crossing skin when they bend went from 3.15 % to 0 % on the bench's villager.
Routes, characters and their limits `/kiln animate` picks the route from the subject, because no single method held up across all of them ([`references/animation.md`](plugin/references/animation.md) has every measurement): | Subject | Route | Shown above | |---|---|---| | Humanoid, a ready-made move | `tools/presets.py` — 22 motions made with NVIDIA Kimodo, retargeted, feet planted and flat | the mascot | | Biped or winged, from a sentence | [UniMate](https://github.com/Friedrich-M/UniMate) text-to-motion, looped by `tools/motion_loop.py` — **non-commercial weights** | the dragon | | Four-legged, idle and walk | `tools/quadruped.py` — a scripted, measured cycle | the cat | | Articulated object | rigid parts keyed by script, every rotation's sign measured first | the lamp, the chest | UniMate was measured **unusable for quadruped walking** — on a cat, a Shiba, a horse and the model author's own robot dog — so a quadruped never goes to it. > **What this showcase is, and is not.** Each UniMate tile is the sample, out of 4, that > `motion_loop.py` kept for looping best, then approved by a reviewer — some prompts tried > (wave, dance, run) were left out. The scripted tiles are deterministic. These come from > scripts (`examples/animation/showcase.sh`), not from an interactive session. ### Organic characters A character is built as **one skin** — families of metaballs or overlapping volumes, joined by a single voxel remesh — so it bends without seams at the shoulders, hips and neck. Then: - **A learned auto-rig.** A humanoid, or a mesh kiln did not build (a generated one), is rigged by [SkinTokens](https://github.com/VAST-AI-Research/SkinTokens) (MIT, runs locally) and handed back with kiln's skeleton: Mixamo names, weights cleaned, eyelid and ear bones added. A quadruped kiln built keeps its own rig, which walked better. On the bench, skin crossing skin when the character bends: **3.15 % → 0 %** on a low-poly villager, **1.34 % → 0 %** on a chibi, **0.74 % → 0.45 %** on a generated humanoid, against 2.2.0's rig. - **Ready-made humanoid moves.** `tools/presets.py` puts 22 motions (walk, run, jump, dance…; 43 clips, NVIDIA Kimodo, commercial use allowed) on a kiln-named humanoid, with the feet planted, the arms kept out of the body, and `--loop` for a closed in-place cycle. - **Looped clips that close** — one clip per file, the last key equal to the first; a walk loop for a game, beside the whole take. Limits, measured: the auto-rig was compared on one pose of two humanoids, and runs differ; a generated humanoid with a hand fused to its hip keeps skin through skin on its arms; SkinTokens needs about 5.6 GB on disk and 7 GB of memory per mesh. `references/characters.md` has every table.
### A GLB from a generator — repaired, lightened, converted Bring the file a generator gave you: kiln inspects it, repairs it, lightens it and converts it. On the bench, a raw TRELLIS output went from 191,520 triangles and 11.4 MB, full of holes, to 9,000 triangles, 0.63 MB, closed — in 16 minutes.
The commands, and what was measured | Command | What it does to your file | |---|---| | `/kiln inspect model.glb` | faces (tris / quads / ngons), vertices, objects, materials, textures and their sizes, bounding box, rig, animations | | `/kiln cleanup` | merge by distance, recalculate normals, remove loose parts, dissolve degenerate faces, check for fused edges, apply transforms, origin at the centre of the base, scale check (1 unit = 1 m), rename to convention, clean orphans, check materials | | (poly count) | reported against the detail tier; past twice its top, a **decimation is proposed with before/after previews — never applied without you**. Thin parts (wires, handles, loops) are rebuilt as curves instead of decimated | | `/kiln texture` | textures a white or untextured mesh — Poly Haven CC0 scans first, procedural second; works on a single fused mesh by grouping faces | | `/kiln optimize model.glb` | textures resized and converted to WebP, Draco geometry compression, or gltfpack simplification and LODs — each shown before/after, kept only if you say so | | `/kiln convert` | GLB ↔ FBX, OBJ → GLB, to USDZ, with the material export audit before any glTF export | | `/kiln animate` | folds bone-parented parts into the skin, checks the rig can bend where asked, then animates ([Animate](#animate-and-characters-that-bend)) | - **A generator's GLB, repaired end to end** (bench brief `repair-trellis-glb`, a raw TRELLIS output): 191,520 triangles, 11.4 MB, 13,732 non-manifold and 10,220 open edges → **9,000 triangles, 0.63 MB, 0 and 0**: the glass globe, too thin to survive a remesh, refilled with a lathe shape fitted to its profile, the whole closed by a voxel remesh and decimated with Blender's Collapse — 16 minutes, $3.89 of API-equivalent usage. On the official Lab MCP: the same 0 and 0, 0.93 MB. - **A generated lantern finished as a game asset** (`ref-lantern-trellis`): shape kept, surface rebuilt, **0.946** against the real lantern's 3D model (2.2.0: 0.934 — [how it is scored](#measured-not-claimed)). - **From a sentence, through the free Hugging Face Spaces** (`ai-mushrooms`): a FLUX.1-schnell concept, then TRELLIS.2 (MIT, one 89 s call), decimated to 8,991 triangles, textured, shipped at 279 KB — 12 minutes, $3.80. kiln 2.2.0 went to Hunyuan3D-2 for the same brief, whose licence excludes the EU, the UK and South Korea; 3.0 uses it only when asked.
### Review rounds — a fresh eye on every model A session that looks at its own model sees what it meant to make. So each model goes through review rounds: six views and a close-up, in colour and in clay, read each round by a new Claude subagent that knows the brief and the photo, never the build. It lists every defect, blocking or detail; the rounds end when two new reviewers in a row find nothing blocking. A prop has no minimum and eight rounds at most; a character or a showcase brief, six at least and twelve at most, then rounds on its motion. Measured after the bench, one run each: on a mascot, the first reviewer found 16 defects the session had passed (a hair flame read as horns, palms without fingers, a bald nape), and the walk no longer snaps the knees; against the real object, the chair from a photo 0.720 → 0.729, the ammo box 0.936 → 0.948 and the lantern 0.885 → 0.888 (eight rounds, the cap: its reviewers disagreed on the tone) — within one session's spread for the scores, so the clearer gain is what the reviewers catch. The price: about twice the time and usage (the ammo box $4.45 → $9.17, the chair $6.64 → $14.39, the lantern $6.04 → $13.19). [`references/review-rounds.md`](plugin/references/review-rounds.md) ### No Blender open — built in the background, several at once Blender closed, or busy with your own work: kiln builds in a background Blender instead, saves the `.blend` there and renders its own check views (two opposite three-quarters, top and under) — the look is never skipped, and the report says the model was built headless. `/kiln batch` makes a series from one manifest, unattended (three props in 7.8 minutes on the bench), and Kiln Studio runs variations up to four at once (Settings → At once). ## Measured, not claimed Each rebuild from a photo is scored against the real 3D object it was photographed from — an asset the session never sees. Blender 5.2.2, Opus 5.5, one run each, October 2026: | Against the real object (1 = identical) | **2.2.0** | **3.0** | 3.0 shipped | Usage (API-equivalent) | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Hurricane lantern, from a photo | 0.900 | 0.885 | 1.18 MB | $6.04 | | The lantern, with a measured template | 0.880 | **0.917** | 474 KB | $7.16 | | The lantern, from a TRELLIS.2 mesh | 0.934 | **0.946** | 465 KB | $6.43 | | Ammo box, from a photo | 0.774 | **0.936** | 373 KB | $4.45 | | Gothic chair, from a photo | 0.637 | **0.720** | 449 KB | $6.64 | The bench ran before [review rounds](#review-rounds--a-fresh-eye-on-every-model). With them, one run each: the lantern 0.888 (612 KB, $13.19), the ammo box 0.948 (493 KB, $9.17) and the chair 0.729 (505 KB, $14.39) — the three shown at the top. Across the whole bench, 3.0 against 2.2.0: both prints pass the printability check (2.2.0: one of two), the humanoids kiln builds no longer pass skin through skin when they bend, and a note in Kiln Studio is addressed in one pass. It costs about 40 % more usage, for the new checks and the work they do.
The whole bench, time per task, and how it is scored | The whole bench — 19 briefs both versions ran, plus Kiln Studio | 2.2.0 | **3.0** | |---|---:|---:| | Briefs that shipped their files | 19 of 19 | 20 of 20 | | Prints passing the printability check (PrusaSlicer second opinion) | 1 of 2 | **2 of 2** | | Rig interpenetration when bent — villager / chibi | 3.15 % / 1.34 % | **0 % / 0 %** | | A note pinned in Kiln Studio, addressed by Claude | — | **passed, $0.69** | | Usage for the 19 briefs (API-equivalent) | $54.06 | $75.87 | | The same 20 briefs on the official Lab MCP | — | 20 of 20, $84.97 | > **About the usage column.** On a Claude Pro or Max subscription, these sessions are > included in your plan's usage — there is nothing extra to pay. The dollar figure is what > the same session would have cost on the Anthropic API (Claude Code's `total_cost_usd`); > the bench uses it to compare versions, and as a rough measure of how much of your plan's > usage a run takes. kiln itself never pays for a service (rule 5). Shape score: mean silhouette overlap with the real asset from front, back, sides and top (`bench/gt_compare.py`); openwork views left out for the chair. Size is assumed when a brief gives none, and a single photo does not give it: every lantern came out 20 to 50 % taller than the real one. One run per brief, and runs of the same skill differ by about ±0.02–0.03. 3.0 costs about 40 % more than 2.2.0: the new checks (render reviews, UV, printability), the learned auto-rig, closed loops and the photo projection are extra work in the session. Three photo briefs and the generator repair were re-run after fixes the bench itself found — what changed and why is in the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md). **Close, not identical, on purpose.** kiln stops at a few dollars of API-equivalent usage per object. [img2threejs](https://github.com/img2threejs/img2threejs), which rebuilds an image as Three.js code through eight vision-reviewed passes, keeps finer surface detail: on the same lantern its likeness was comparable — 0.866 against kiln v7's 0.861 (2.0 era) — at about three times the usage, estimated on a run stopped after three of its eight passes ([benchmarks § 4](docs/benchmarks.md#4-kiln-against-an-image-to-code-tool)). What did not improve is published too: the [benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md) — eighteen versions of one lantern, what each fix broke, how the bench was kept honest — and every number, render and GLB under 1 MB on the [`bench-results`](https://github.com/elithril/blender-kiln/tree/bench-results) branch, except the humanoid derived from Hunyuan3D, whose licence keeps it out. ### How long it takes Time Claude spent on whole headless sessions in the bench (auto mode, every question answered in the brief, so no time waiting for you), Blender 5.2.2, skill 3.0, one run each, October 2026. Describe an object, or show a photo of it, and get back a clean 3D model you can edit, ship in a game or on the web, animate, or print.

kiln is a Claude Code skill on top of a Blender MCP server. The MCP server gives Claude

hands in Blender; kiln gives it the production method — sourcing, modelling, cleanup,

texturing from CC0 scans, optimization, validation, export — and measures the file it

ships. It runs on both servers: ahujasid's mcp-for-blender

and the Blender Foundation's official Blender Lab MCP,

the server behind Claude's Blender connector.

<sub>Cited in <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01057"><i>3DCodeBench: Benchmarking Agentic Procedural 3D Modeling Via Code</i></a> (Google DeepMind, USC, 2026), §1.</sub>

Quickstart


/plugin marketplace add elithril/blender-kiln

/plugin install blender-kiln@blender-kiln

/kiln setup

/kiln A hanging iron lantern for a medieval inn, stylized, for the web

/kiln setup detects Blender, the MCP server and the optional tools, and says what is

missing — see [Requirements](#requirements). Then, for example:


/kiln Rebuild the lamp in ./lamp.png as a game asset

/kiln optimize ./generated.glb               # a GLB from anywhere: lighter, checked

/kiln animate SK_Cat.glb walk, idle

/kiln A 90 mm windmill for my FDM printer

/kiln studio                                 # look at the models, pin notes, let Claude act on them

A local page that shows every model in your project. Pin a note on a spot — *"the ring is too

small to hang it"* — press Work on it with Claude, and the change lands in the model, with

Claude's reply and a before/after on the note. Studio also exports for games and AR in seconds,

and shows the model in AR on your iPhone through a QR code. From the terminal, Claude sees the

model you have open in Studio and can turn it, compare it and present it on a second screen.

Measured: a note addressed in one pass, nothing else moved, for $0.69 of API-equivalent usage.

<details>

<summary><b>Everything Studio does</b></summary>

A local page for looking at what kiln made, telling it what to change, and asking Claude from

the page itself. /kiln studio starts it on your project folder (or reuses the one running):

every .glb .gltf .fbx .obj .usdz .3mf .stl under it shows up, and kiln's _original …

_final stages are one model you can switch between.

  • Look — Lit, Unlit, Clay, Normals, UV checker, Faces (back faces red), wireframe, sizes in

metres, bones, animation clips with a scrubber; the previous version beside the current one.

  • Annotate — pin a note on a spot (it records the point in Blender coordinates, the object

and material hit, the camera, a screenshot and a close-up) or write one about the whole model.

  • Ask Claude from the page — with "Ask Claude from Studio" on, the page runs Claude Code

itself (claude -p, on its own Blender, never yours): "Work on them with Claude" addresses

every open note, a conversation per model and one for the project, *New model* asks for a model

from a sentence or a photo. Safe calls pass; anything else waits for your OK in the page, and

paid generation asks unless you set it to Auto in Settings. Measured on the bench: a note asking for a ring twice as big,

addressed in one pass — ×1.9, nothing else moved, the note answered — for $0.69 of

API-equivalent usage (official Lab MCP: $0.73). Or run /kiln studio in your terminal: Claude

reads the open notes, changes the model, re-exports and replies on each.

  • Claude in your terminal sees what Studio shows — installed as a plugin, kiln brings a small

MCP server, kiln-studio, with nothing more to set up (a standalone-skill clone does not

register it). Say *"fix this"* or *"what am I looking at"* and Claude reads

the model open in the page, its stage, the camera and the note picked, and can grab the image

you see. It drives the page too: open a model, turn the view to a note's, switch to clay or

normals, a before/after against the previous version, play a clip, and a present mode for a

second screen. It replies on notes and leaves its own, and makes variations and finishes when

you ask; it never touches a model file itself. Tools and when they are called:

[references/studio.md § 11](plugin/references/studio.md#11-the-kiln-studio-mcp-server--what-the-user-is-looking-at-and-driving-studio).

  • Outputs — Web, Game, AR and 3D print for each model. Game (FBX) and AR (a GLB and a USDZ

that passes usdchecker --arkit) are made by Studio itself, in seconds, without Claude.

*Download* zips the outputs you pick with a sheet: each file's size and use, the licences.

  • On your phone — a QR code shows the model in AR on an iPhone (AR Quick Look), on the same

Wi-Fi, through a read-only link that expires after 15 minutes. Android: not tried yet.

  • Variations and finishes — new models from a copy of this one ("the same in rusted iron"),

one Claude run each, several at once if you allow it; finishes are kept in one file

(KHR_materials_variants) and the AR view lets you pick one.

  • Check — the Checks tab reads the file in plain words, each with how to fix it: triangles

against the detail tier, size and ground contact, texture sizes, compression, the licences

the log records, and the fidelity measure against the reference photo.

  • Watch it built — once the brief is confirmed, the page opens the model kiln is building

and reloads it after each phase; a dot per model shows what kiln is on.

  • Every command by name (⌘K), seven themes (high contrast among them), English and French, a

playable tutorial on an example model, a tip the first time you meet each feature.

with the models. [references/studio.md](plugin/references/studio.md) is the reference.

Say it will be printed — FDM or resin, a height, your printer's colours — and kiln models for the

printer from the first primitive: closed solids at size, walls thick enough, a flat base, parts

that fit together, one file per colour. Every file is checked, with PrusaSlicer as a second

opinion. In the bench, the 3.0 passed both prints the 2.2.0 had half-failed; four objects kiln

modelled were printed as exported, on a Bambu Lab P1S.

<details>

<summary><b>How print mode works, and its limits</b></summary>

Say it will be printed — FDM or resin, a height, your printer's colours — and kiln models

for the printer from the first primitive: at size, in closed solids joined into one

volume, walls thick enough (0.8 mm FDM, 0.5 mm resin), a flat base, overhangs designed out

where nobody looks, relief as geometry, and in several parts when one would print in the

air — the windmill above is a body and its sails, laid flat, each checked on its own. STL in

millimetres. Every STL ends with [tools/print_check.py](plugin/tools/print_check.py): open and

non-manifold edges, normals, held and floating parts, walls, overhangs, loss against the

original, the smallest scale you can shrink it to in the slicer, and PrusaSlicer as a

second opinion ([references/print.md](plugin/references/print.md)).

<p align="center">

<img src="docs/images/print-teapot.webp" width="100%" alt="A museum photo of an 18th-century drum teapot, and the printable model kiln built from it: body, spout rings, ribbed lid, diamonds and zigzags engraved 0.6 mm deep to paint" />

</p>

Measured on sessions given the skill and nothing else: a dog house and a lighthouse from a

brief, a pumpkin and a ghost from photos, the windmill, and this teapot from three museum

photos — printable, and like what was asked.

Stylised figures, not likenesses. Two cats — one held by the ghost, one from a real cat's

photo — passed every check and were unacceptable to look at. A stylised figure is another

matter: a session made a cartoon dragon from one flat drawing, in four colour parts, from

metaball families and one voxel remesh, and a fresh session then made a cartoon fox the

same way. So print mode builds a stylised figure that way, and says at CONFIG that a

realistic likeness of a real animal or person is out of reach of scripted modelling.

A model you made: flatten it, then check it

<p align="center">

<img src="docs/images/print-flatten-prusaslicer.svg" width="100%" alt="What PrusaSlicer lays down for the windmill turned 1 degree with 10 percent of its vertices off: the gallery floor's top layer in 4 heights and one edge of the base on the bed; after flatten.py, one height and the whole base" />

</p>

A model finished by hand often has faces that should be flat and are not, and sits a degree

off. [tools/flatten.py](plugin/tools/flatten.py) makes nearly flat faces exactly flat and lays the

base on the bed — on the windmill above, 629 mm of first layer become 3,317 — and touches

nothing else: curves, folds, bevels and real slopes stay, no vertex moves past the tolerance,

the input is never overwritten.


/kiln inspect model.stl     # print mode: print_check's verdict

/kiln cleanup model.stl     # print mode: flatten.py, then print_check again, before and after shown

Limits

  • Printed, four of them. The forge, the lighthouse, the Art Deco box and the windmill were

printed as kiln exported them, on a Bambu Lab P1S in PLA ([photos](#3d-printing--models-that-actually-print)).

The box's bayonet lid turns, locks and holds with the box upside down. The fit test print was not printed; the

rest was checked by PrusaSlicer 2.9.6 and by renders, not on a bed.

  • FDM, checked with PrusaSlicer's default profile. No resin slicing, no orientation search,

no support generation, no build-volume check.

  • Scaled down in the slicer, a model loses its thin walls. print_check says how far —

"do not shrink below 40 %" for the windmill's body, 67 % for the lighthouse.

  • Parts are glued or pressed, never moving. 0.2 mm a side is a usual clearance, not

measured here; [tools/fit_coupon.py](plugin/tools/fit_coupon.py) writes the test print that

measures it on your printer.

  • Decorative objects, not mechanical parts. A bracket, or a box whose lid must close, belongs

in a CAD tool (build123d, CadQuery, OpenSCAD).

  • No multi-material file. A colour is painted, or printed as its own part.
  • Self-intersections are counted, not repaired, and flatten.py does not fill holes.

The full list is in [references/print.md](plugin/references/print.md) § What it does not check.

The teapot photo is the Auckland War Memorial Museum's, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

</details>

From a photo — rebuilt in Blender, measured against the real object

<p align="center">

<img src="docs/images/how-it-works.webp" alt="Five steps from a real session on an ammo box: the photo read in crops, eight scanned textures compared, the silhouette overlay, every joint rendered, the shipped GLB" width="100%" />

</p>

<p align="center"><sub>Every panel is a file the session itself wrote while rebuilding the ammo box above — nothing re-staged.</sub></p>

Give it a photo and kiln rebuilds the object by script, textures it from CC0 scans, and measures

its silhouette and materials against the photo before shipping. Against the real 3D object the

photo was taken of: an ammo box at 0.948 with review rounds (0.936 on the bench, before them), a

hurricane lantern at 0.888 (0.885 before them), 0.946 when kiln finishes a TRELLIS.2 mesh of the

photo ([the numbers](#measured-not-claimed)).

<details>

<summary><b>The five steps</b></summary>

1. Read the photo before modeling. An inventory of every part and how it meets the next,

from enlarged crops; the real size, the camera's height and angle — asked, or stated as

assumptions. Given a 3D mesh generated from the same photo, its proportions are measured

instead ([TRELLIS.2, locally](plugin/references/ai-generation.md)) — never shipped.

2. Texture from scans, not noise. A Poly Haven CC0 texture set of the material family,

chosen by eye against the photo, tinted to its palette, worn by the form.

3. Measure against the photo. [plugin/tools/fidelity_check.py](plugin/tools/fidelity_check.py) renders

the model at the photo's camera under a studio light and lists the gaps — silhouette per

height band, materials, metal that cannot exist.

4. Look at every joint. Each end of a long part that touches another is rendered alone: a

part that joins another enters it.

5. Ship, and measure the file that ships. Optimized (Draco, WebP), validated, re-measured

as a GLB — what the user gets, not the .blend.

</details>

Organic characters

A character is built as one skin — families of metaballs or overlapping volumes, joined by

a single voxel remesh — so it bends without seams at the shoulders, hips and neck. Then:

  • A learned auto-rig. A humanoid, or a mesh kiln did not build (a generated one), is rigged

by SkinTokens (MIT, runs locally) and handed

back with kiln's skeleton: Mixamo names, weights cleaned, eyelid and ear bones added. A

quadruped kiln built keeps its own rig, which walked better. On the bench, skin crossing skin

when the character bends: 3.15 % → 0 % on a low-poly villager, 1.34 % → 0 % on a chibi,

0.74 % → 0.45 % on a generated humanoid, against 2.2.0's rig.

  • Ready-made humanoid moves. tools/presets.py puts 22 motions (walk, run, jump, dance…;

43 clips, NVIDIA Kimodo, commercial use allowed) on a kiln-named humanoid, with the feet

planted, the arms kept out of the body, and --loop for a closed in-place cycle.

  • Looped clips that close — one clip per file, the last key equal to the first; a walk loop

for a game, beside the whole take.

Limits, measured: the auto-rig was compared on one pose of two humanoids, and runs differ; a

generated humanoid with a hand fused to its hip keeps skin through skin on its arms; SkinTokens

needs about 5.6 GB on disk and 7 GB of memory per mesh. references/characters.md has every

table.

</details>

A GLB from a generator — repaired, lightened, converted

Bring the file a generator gave you: kiln inspects it, repairs it, lightens it and converts it.

On the bench, a raw TRELLIS output went from 191,520 triangles and 11.4 MB, full of holes, to

9,000 triangles, 0.63 MB, closed — in 16 minutes.

<details>

<summary><b>The commands, and what was measured</b></summary>

| Command | What it does to your file |

|---|---|

| /kiln inspect model.glb | faces (tris / quads / ngons), vertices, objects, materials, textures and their sizes, bounding box, rig, animations |

| /kiln cleanup | merge by distance, recalculate normals, remove loose parts, dissolve degenerate faces, check for fused edges, apply transforms, origin at the centre of the base, scale check (1 unit = 1 m), rename to convention, clean orphans, check materials |

| (poly count) | reported against the detail tier; past twice its top, a decimation is proposed with before/after previews — never applied without you. Thin parts (wires, handles, loops) are rebuilt as curves instead of decimated |

| /kiln texture | textures a white or untextured mesh — Poly Haven CC0 scans first, procedural second; works on a single fused mesh by grouping faces |

| /kiln optimize model.glb | textures resized and converted to WebP, Draco geometry compression, or gltfpack simplification and LODs — each shown before/after, kept only if you say so |

| /kiln convert | GLB ↔ FBX, OBJ → GLB, to USDZ, with the material export audit before any glTF export |

| /kiln animate | folds bone-parented parts into the skin, checks the rig can bend where asked, then animates ([Animate](#animate-and-characters-that-bend)) |

  • A generator's GLB, repaired end to end (bench brief repair-trellis-glb, a raw TRELLIS

output): 191,520 triangles, 11.4 MB, 13,732 non-manifold and 10,220 open edges → **9,000

triangles, 0.63 MB, 0 and 0**: the glass globe, too thin to survive a remesh, refilled with a

lathe shape fitted to its profile, the whole closed by a voxel remesh and decimated with

Blender's Collapse — 16 minutes, $3.89 of API-equivalent usage. On the official

Lab MCP: the same 0 and 0, 0.93 MB.

  • A generated lantern finished as a game asset (ref-lantern-trellis): shape kept, surface

rebuilt, 0.946 against the real lantern's 3D model (2.2.0: 0.934 — [how it is scored](#measured-not-claimed)).

  • From a sentence, through the free Hugging Face Spaces (ai-mushrooms): a FLUX.1-schnell

concept, then TRELLIS.2 (MIT, one 89 s call), decimated to 8,991 triangles, textured, shipped at

279 KB — 12 minutes, $3.80. kiln 2.2.0 went to Hunyuan3D-2 for the same brief, whose licence

excludes the EU, the UK and South Korea; 3.0 uses it only when asked.

</details>

Review rounds — a fresh eye on every model

A session that looks at its own model sees what it meant to make. So each model goes through

review rounds: six views and a close-up, in colour and in clay, read each round by a new Claude

subagent that knows the brief and the photo, never the build. It lists every defect, blocking or

detail; the rounds end when two new reviewers in a row find nothing blocking. A prop has no

minimum and eight rounds at most; a character or a showcase brief, six at least and twelve at

most, then rounds on its motion.

Measured after the bench, one run each: on a mascot, the first reviewer found 16 defects the

session had passed (a hair flame read as horns, palms without fingers, a bald nape), and the walk

no longer snaps the knees; against the real object, the chair from a photo 0.720 → 0.729, the

ammo box 0.936 → 0.948 and the lantern 0.885 → 0.888 (eight rounds, the cap: its reviewers

disagreed on the tone) — within one session's spread for the scores, so the clearer gain is what

the reviewers catch. The price: about twice the time and usage (the ammo box $4.45 → $9.17, the

chair $6.64 → $14.39, the lantern $6.04 → $13.19). [references/review-rounds.md](plugin/references/review-rounds.md)

No Blender open — built in the background, several at once

Blender closed, or busy with your own work: kiln builds in a background Blender instead, saves

the .blend there and renders its own check views (two opposite three-quarters, top and under)

— the look is never skipped, and the report says the model was built headless. /kiln batch

makes a series from one manifest, unattended (three props in 7.8 minutes on the bench), and

Kiln Studio runs variations up to four at once (Settings → At once).

Close, not identical, on purpose. kiln stops at a few dollars of API-equivalent usage per object.

likeness was comparable — 0.866 against kiln v7's 0.861 (2.0 era) — at about three times the usage, estimated on

a run stopped after three of its eight passes

# blender-kiln — The 3D Asset Forge

You are a 3D asset production expert. You pilot Blender via MCP to produce clean, optimized assets from brief to export.

Keep every working file — scripts, crops, renders, bakes — inside the asset's output
folder. Never write to `/tmp` or any shared path under a generic name: a bench session
wrote `/tmp/top.png` and could not tell whether it had overwritten someone's file.

Reply in the language the user wrote the request in — not the language of the machine, its paths or its locale. Measured: two bench sessions answered in French to an English brief.

---

| `/kiln batch` | Batch wizard → manifest → autonomous multi-asset production |
| `/kiln batch run` | Execute/resume a batch manifest (options: `--all`, `--asset <name>`) |

### Argument routing

above arrives as the skill's arguments. Route on the FIRST word:

Load `references/texturing-strategy.md`. With a reference image, also `references/reference-fidelity.md` § 4 — **start from a scanned CC0 texture set (Poly Haven) when the material family has one**, look at its thumbnail against the photo's crop, tint it to the photo's palette, wear it with a second set masked by the form, bake to UVs —; one material per region, a palette sampled from the image, independent colour / roughness / relief fields with grime along the part's direction, relief baked to a normal map, and the glass recipe.

**Strategies in order of proposal:**

1. **Geometric analysis + PolyHaven** — analyze face normals/position/curvature, cluster into zones, label visually, search PolyHaven textures per zone, apply PBR materials. If reference image available, use it to match textures to zones (e.g. wood grain visible on top → wood PBR on horizontal faces)
2. **Procedural Blender materials** — for stylized/cartoon/low-poly, Principled BSDF with values only, no image textures. If reference image available, extract colors and finish (matte/glossy) from it
3. **Assisted manual texturing** — skill prepares UVs + material slots, user textures manually
4. **Try another Space** — if current Space doesn't support texture, offer to change URL

  → `tools/presets.py`; other biped or wings → UniMate (non-commercial, asked first);
  articulated object → keys. `references/animation.md` § Rules for scripted animation.

### [6] OPTIMIZE and [7] EXPORT — `references/pipeline-optimize-export.md`

- OPTIMIZE, auto mode, glTF: textures to WebP at 1024 (2048 only when asked), then Draco,
  as separate steps (rule 20), without asking; `_original.glb` kept, plus
  `{name}_preview.glb` (no Draco, no WebP: the Mac's Quick Look opens it). **`_final.glb`
  exists only after this phase.** Simplify, decimate, LOD: always interactive. Print: skipped.
- Each output in its own folder: `web/`, `game/`, `ar/`, `print/`; the source at the root.
- EXPORT: `references/export-targets.md`; material audit before any glTF (rule 19), never
  `export_apply=True` (rule 18). Print: `print_check` **PASS required**. Save the .blend
  (rules 7, 16). Interactive: `studio.py live <name> --end`, then `studio.py checks <name>`
  and report its WARN lines.

## Blender MCP

ahujasid's server is `mcp-for-blender` (formerly `blender-mcp`). Since 2.1.9 it serves nine
tools; the rules name them: `get_addon_status`, `get_scene_info` (with `size`, `ground`,
`topology` fields), `look` (framed views, rules 2 and 22), `execute_blender_code`,
`search_assets` / `import_asset` (PolyHaven, Sketchfab, Poly Pizza), `generate_3d` (paid
providers, rule 5), and telemetry, left off.

- First call of a session: `get_addon_status()` — `up_to_date`, and which `libraries` and
  `generators` are on (rule 23).
- Always go through the MCP tools, never the addon's raw socket.
- **Other tools than these** — `get_viewport_screenshot`, `get_object_info` (mcp-for-blender
  2.1.3 or older), or `get_objects_summary` (the official Blender Lab MCP): read
  `references/blender-mcp.md` before the first phase. It maps every rule to their names.

## Multi-Asset Sessions

```
First asset:  full CONFIG → pipeline [1] to [7]
Next assets:  "Next asset?" → reuse CONFIG → resume at [2] BRIEF
```
